taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes Starkey et al. (2003) recognised C. dorsalis (southern painted turtle) as a separate species, while some herpetologists keep it in C. picta; NatureServe lists three subspecies (bellii, marginata, picta).
fieldMarks: Smooth, relatively flat, unkeeled shell, 4-8 in (about 9-25 cm), with a non-serrated rear edge; olive-green to brown or black with thin red or orange lines and red edges on the marginals.
Skin olive to black with yellow stripes on the head, neck, limbs and tail; yellow eyes with a dark bar through the pupil.
Plastron is red or orange with dark markings that fade with age (a large grey 'oak leaf' blotch in the western form).
Males are smaller than females, with thicker tails and elongated foreclaws.
behavior: Diurnal; basks in large groups on logs and rocks (sometimes 50 stacked on one log) and dives quickly at danger.
Active about March (late April-May in the far north) to October; overwinters buried in mud at the bottom of wetlands.
Omnivore eating plants, algae, aquatic insects, fish and crustaceans, feeding only in water.
habitat: Slow-moving, shallow fresh water with soft bottoms and dense aquatic vegetation: marshes, ponds, shallow lake bays, slow rivers and backwaters.
Needs basking sites; nests in soft soil up to several hundred metres from water.
range: Only turtle spanning North America coast to coast: from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick across southern Canada to Vancouver Island, and through most of the eastern and central US to the Gulf Coast in Louisiana; a few isolated populations occur in the southwest US and Mexico.
